summary: An early Telnet option, from 1974, for negotiating how linefeed characters in output are handled. Different systems treated line endings differently, so the option lets both ends settle on a convention. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 658 defines a TELNET option for deciding how a connection handles output linefeeds. It lets the sender and receiver negotiate who handles them and whether to delay, discard or simulate them.

subtitle: A TELNET option for negotiating which side handles linefeeds in output.

tldr.problem: A sender and receiver may need to agree on which side handles output linefeeds and whether to delay, discard or simulate them.
tldr.mechanism: The NAOLFD TELNET option uses option code 16 and an 8-bit value in subnegotiation to propose who handles linefeeds and how.
tldr.outcome: RFC 658 is Historic. It defines a default negotiation state and rules for resolving which side handles output linefeeds.

today: RFC 658 is Historic. The unit lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Negotiating Output Linefeed Handling
sections.content:
NAOLFD means “Negotiate About Output Linefeed Disposition” and has TELNET option code 16. The option applies to a simplex connection with a data sender and a data receiver. The usual DO, DON'T, WILL and WON'T commands request, accept or refuse negotiation.

After agreement, and without further subnegotiation, the receiver is assumed to handle output linefeeds. The default is DON'T NAOLFD and WON'T NAOLFD; in that unnegotiated state neither side is required or prohibited from handling them, though the RFC says it is appropriate for at least the receiver to do so.
sections.plainLanguage: The option lets the sender and receiver agree on who handles linefeeds in output. If they do not negotiate, the receiver is the expected place to handle them.

sections.title: The Subnegotiation Value
sections.content:
Subnegotiation uses an 8-bit value. Value 0 says the command sender alone will handle linefeeds. Values 1 through 250 ask the other party to handle them with a delay measured in character-times or inserted NULs. Value 251 is not allowed; 252 suggests discarding linefeeds, 253 suggests simulating them, 254 suggests waiting for a character on the other simplex connection, and 255 makes no suggestion about how to handle them.

The sender's subnegotiation code is DS with value 1, and the receiver's is DR with value 0. The sender must place any delay NULs immediately after the character.
sections.plainLanguage: The value tells the other side who should handle linefeeds and what to do. For example, it can request a delay, discarding or simulation.

sections.title: How Conflicting Preferences Are Resolved
sections.content:
If neither sender nor receiver wants to handle output linefeeds, the receiver must do it. If both want to handle them, the sender does, because the RFC assumes it has special knowledge about the data and can take the receiver's suggestions into account.

Linefeed simulation replaces a linefeed with a new-line and enough blanks to return the print head or line pointer to its prior horizontal position. Simulation is allowed only when the linefeed is not immediately preceded by a carriage return. The RFC notes that padding must be applied to all linefeeds when selected.
sections.plainLanguage: If both sides want to handle linefeeds, the sender's choice takes priority. If neither does, the receiver handles them.
